title: System Overview
text:
The HAR Distributed Framework is a multi-node wearable computing architecture developed for Human Activity Recognition (HAR) using distributed embedded processing.
Instead of continuously transmitting all raw wearable sensor measurements to a single computer for processing, the framework distributes part of the classification workload among multiple embedded edge devices.
Each edge node processes information from a wearable sensor, performs local neural network inference, and generates a probability distribution over the supported activity classes.
These local predictions are transmitted to a central computing node, where they are temporally synchronized and combined to generate the final system-level activity prediction.

title: System Overview
text:
System Architecture
The framework is organized into four main computational layers:

Wearable sensing
Edge inference
Communication and synchronization
Central prediction fusion

The overall processing flow can be summarized as:





This architecture separates sensor-level processing from system-level decision making. Local models perform inference close to the sensing source, while the central node combines the information generated by all distributed nodes.

title: System Overview
text:
Main System Components
The framework consists of three main hardware and computational groups:

Wearable Sensor Nodes
Wearable inertial sensors are placed at multiple body locations to capture motion and orientation information during human activities.
The distributed configuration uses five sensing locations:

Chest
Left Hand
Right Hand
Left Knee
Right Knee

Each sensing stream is associated with an embedded computing node responsible for receiving sensor measurements, preparing the model input, and performing local inference.
The wearable sensors provide inertial and orientation information that represents the movement of different regions of the body.


Edge Computing Nodes
The edge computing nodes execute trained local Human Activity Recognition models using the data received from their corresponding wearable sensors.
The real-time system operates using fixed input windows of 50 samples.
Once a complete window is available, the local neural network processes the sensor data and produces a probability distribution over the supported activity classes.
Conceptually, the local model output can be represented as:
[p0, p1, p2, p3, p4, p5]
where each value represents the probability associated with one activity class.
Rather than continuously forwarding the complete raw sensor stream to the central device, the edge nodes transmit these local prediction probabilities.


Central Computing Node
The central computing node receives predictions generated independently by all edge nodes.
Its main responsibilities include:

receiving local probability vectors;
temporally aligning predictions from different nodes;
handling temporarily unavailable predictions;
combining local probability vectors;
executing the central fusion model;
generating the global activity prediction;
recording timing and synchronization information; and
forwarding prediction results to the visualization interface.

title: System Overview
text:
System Data Flow
The complete data flow of the distributed HAR framework follows the sequence below:

Wearable sensors acquire motion and orientation measurements.
Sensor measurements are transferred to their corresponding edge computing nodes.
Each edge node buffers the incoming data.
A fixed-length input window is constructed.
The local HAR model performs neural network inference.
Each local model generates an activity probability vector.
The probability vector is transmitted through the communication network.
The central node receives predictions generated by the distributed edge nodes.
Predictions from different nodes are temporally synchronized.
The synchronized probability vectors are provided to the central fusion model.
The fusion model generates a global activity probability distribution.
The final activity prediction is obtained.
Prediction, communication, timing, and synchronization information can be recorded for subsequent analysis.
The global prediction can also be forwarded to the graphical visualization interface.

title: System Overview
text:
Distributed Processing Strategy
A fundamental characteristic of the framework is the separation between local inference and global decision making.
At the edge level, each embedded node processes information associated with a specific wearable sensing location.
At the central level, the system combines the predictions produced by the distributed nodes.
The computational strategy can therefore be represented as two processing stages:
Sensor-Level Processing
        │
        ▼
Local Predictions
        │
        ▼
System-Level Processing
        │
        ▼
Global Prediction
This organization allows the framework to distribute the computational workload across multiple embedded devices while maintaining a central mechanism for system-level activity recognition.

title: System Overview
text:
Probability-Level Communication
Communication between the edge nodes and the central node is performed at the prediction level.
The local edge devices perform inference before communicating with the central system.
The basic communication principle is:
Wearable Sensor
       │
       ▼
Local Edge Device
       │
       ▼
Local HAR Model
       │
       ▼
Probability Vector
       │
       ▼
Communication Network
       │
       ▼
Central Computing Node
Therefore, the communication framework exchanges model outputs rather than continuously transmitting complete raw sensor windows for centralized inference.
The implementation details of the communication protocol, message structure, ROS topics, timestamps, and sequence information are described later in the documentation.

title: System Overview
text:
Prediction Synchronization
Local predictions are generated by independent embedded nodes and may not arrive at the central device at exactly the same instant.
The framework therefore includes mechanisms for temporally coordinating the predictions before they are used by the central fusion model.
Under normal operating conditions, predictions generated by the different nodes are grouped according to their timestamps using approximate temporal synchronization.
The system also includes a mechanism for maintaining operation when a prediction from one or more distributed nodes is temporarily unavailable.
The detailed implementation of the synchronization mechanisms is documented separately.

title: System Overview
System Overview
text:
Central Prediction Fusion
Once local predictions have been received and synchronized, they are provided to the central fusion model.
Conceptually, the fusion process can be represented as:
Chest Probabilities ────────────┐
Left Hand Probabilities ────────┤
Right Hand Probabilities ───────┤
Left Knee Probabilities ────────┤──► Fusion Model ───► Global Prediction
Right Knee Probabilities ───────┘
The central model combines the information generated from different body locations and produces a single probability distribution representing the global system prediction.
The architecture, training procedure, input organization, and deployment of the fusion model are described in the model development section of this documentation.

title: System Overview
text:
Real-Time System Outputs
The final global prediction can be consumed by multiple components of the framework.

Experiment Logging
The system records information required to analyze its behavior during real-time execution.
This includes information associated with:

local predictions;
global predictions;
inference timing;
communication timing;
synchronization;
sequence information; and
experiment execution.

These records are later used for quantitative evaluation of the distributed framework.


Visualization Interface
The global activity prediction is also made available to a graphical visualization interface.
The interface allows the predicted activities and system outputs to be observed while the distributed framework is operating.
The implementation and configuration of the visualization system are documented in a dedicated section.

title: Hardware Overview
text:
The HAR Distributed Framework was implemented using a heterogeneous hardware architecture composed of wearable sensing devices, embedded edge computing platforms, a central computing node, and a dedicated wireless communication network.
The hardware infrastructure supports the complete distributed Human Activity Recognition (HAR) pipeline, including sensor acquisition, local neural network inference, inter-node communication, central prediction fusion, experiment logging, and real-time visualization.

title: Hardware Overview
text:
Hardware Architecture
The physical implementation of the framework can be divided into four main hardware groups:

Wearable sensing devices
Edge computing nodes
Central computing node
Network infrastructure

The general hardware organization is:
                     HUMAN SUBJECT
                          │
                          ▼
               Wearable Motion Sensors
                          │
                          │ Bluetooth
                          ▼
              Embedded Edge Computing
                          │
                          │ Wi-Fi
                          ▼
               Dedicated Local Network
                          │
                          ▼
                Central Computing Node
                    │             │
                    ▼             ▼
                 Logging      Visualization
The wearable sensors capture body motion at different anatomical locations. Each sensor communicates with an associated embedded edge computer, where sensor-specific processing and local HAR inference are performed.
The resulting predictions are transmitted through the local wireless network to the central computing platform.

title: Hardware Overview
text:
Wearable Sensors
The sensing layer of the framework uses MbientLab MetaMotionRL wearable devices.
The devices used in the experimental system correspond to the MetaMotionRL r0.5 platform.
These wearable sensors provide inertial and orientation measurements that can be used to characterize human movement.
The distributed configuration uses five body locations:



Sensor Node
Body Location




Chest
Chest


Left Hand
Left hand


Right Hand
Right hand


Left Knee
Left knee


Right Knee
Right knee



The placement of sensors at different body locations provides complementary information about upper-body, lower-body, and torso motion.

Sensor Modalities
Depending on the sensing node and experimental configuration, the framework uses inertial or orientation information.
The primary signal representations used throughout the project include:

accelerometer measurements;
gyroscope measurements; and
quaternion-based orientation measurements.

Accelerometer and gyroscope streams can be represented as:
ax, ay, az, gx, gy, gz
while quaternion orientation is represented as:
w, x, y, z
The exact signal configuration used by each model is described later in the data acquisition and model development sections.


Sensor Communication
Each wearable sensing device communicates wirelessly with its corresponding edge computing node.
The wearable-to-edge connection is based on Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE).
This creates the first communication stage of the distributed architecture:
MetaMotionRL
     │
     │ BLE
     ▼
Edge Computing Node
Sensor acquisition therefore occurs locally at each embedded computing node before any information is exchanged through the distributed network.

title: Hardware Overview
text:
Edge Computing Nodes
The distributed processing layer is implemented using NVIDIA Jetson embedded computing platforms.
The framework has been developed and evaluated using devices from the Jetson family, including:

NVIDIA Jetson Nano
NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano

Five edge computing nodes are associated with the five wearable sensing locations:
Chest Sensor
     │
     ▼
Chest Edge Node


Left Hand Sensor
     │
     ▼
Left Hand Edge Node


Right Hand Sensor
     │
     ▼
Right Hand Edge Node


Left Knee Sensor
     │
     ▼
Left Knee Edge Node


Right Knee Sensor
     │
     ▼
Right Knee Edge Node
Each edge node is responsible for the processing associated with one wearable sensor stream.

Edge Node Responsibilities
The primary responsibilities of each embedded edge device include:

establishing communication with the wearable sensor;
acquiring incoming sensor measurements;
buffering sensor samples;
constructing model input windows;
preprocessing data when required;
executing the local HAR neural network;
generating activity probability vectors;
timestamping local predictions;
publishing predictions to the communication network; and
recording local timing information when required.

The local processing pipeline can therefore be summarized as:
MetaMotionRL
     │
     │ BLE
     ▼
Sensor Acquisition
     │
     ▼
Sample Buffer
     │
     ▼
Input Window
     │
     ▼
Local Neural Network
     │
     ▼
Probability Vector
     │
     ▼
Network Transmission


Local Input Window
The real-time inference pipeline operates using windows containing 50 samples.
At a nominal acquisition rate of 50 Hz, a complete 50-sample input window represents approximately:
50 samples / 50 samples per second = 1 second
of sensor information.
Once the required number of samples is available, the local model performs inference and generates the corresponding class probability vector.

title: Hardware Overview
text:
Central Computing Node
A separate NVIDIA embedded computing platform acts as the central node of the distributed framework.
The primary central platform used for the distributed real-time system is the:
NVIDIA Jetson AGX Xavier
Unlike the edge nodes, the central computing node does not directly perform the sensor-specific local classification tasks.
Instead, it receives the outputs generated by the distributed classifiers and performs system-level processing.

Central Node Responsibilities
The central node is responsible for:

receiving local prediction messages;
managing predictions from multiple edge devices;
temporally synchronizing distributed predictions;
detecting missing or delayed inputs;
applying fallback mechanisms when required;
executing the central fusion model;
generating the global HAR prediction;
recording communication and synchronization metrics;
recording inference and end-to-end timing information; and
transmitting results to the visualization interface.

The central processing sequence is:
Edge Predictions
       │
       ▼
Network Reception
       │
       ▼
Synchronization
       │
       ▼
Prediction Fusion
       │
       ▼
Global HAR Prediction
       │
       ├──────────► Logging
       │
       └──────────► Visualization

text:
Network Infrastructure
Communication between the embedded computing nodes is performed through a dedicated wireless local area network.
The experimental framework uses a:
Ubiquiti Dream Router 7
as the central network infrastructure connecting the distributed Jetson devices.
The network supports communication between:

the five distributed edge nodes;
the central computing node; and
additional systems involved in monitoring or visualization when required.

The overall communication structure is:
Edge Node 1 ──┐
Edge Node 2 ──┤
Edge Node 3 ──┤
Edge Node 4 ──┤──► Wi-Fi Router ◄──► Central Node
Edge Node 5 ──┘
A dedicated local network reduces dependence on external network infrastructure and provides a controlled environment for measuring communication behavior.
The detailed IP configuration, ROS networking configuration, and communication protocol are described later in the documentation.

title: Hardware Overview
text:
Hardware Summary
The distributed framework uses a physically distributed architecture consisting of:

5 MetaMotionRL wearable sensors;
5 embedded edge computing nodes;
1 central NVIDIA Jetson AGX Xavier; and
1 dedicated wireless router.

The resulting system contains six embedded computing devices participating in the inference architecture:
5 Edge Computing Nodes
          +
1 Central Computing Node
          =
6 Embedded Computing Nodes
The five edge devices perform local sensor-level inference, while the central device performs synchronization and prediction fusion.
This hardware organization provides the physical foundation for the distributed processing strategy described in the System Overview.

title: Expansion Via M.2 Slot On Carrier Board And SSD
text:
SSD, also known as Solid State Drives, is often used as the primary storage device for laptops, desktops, etc. With its high reliability and fast data read and write rates, it is the best choice for reComputer expansion.




Device used for this example was reComputeJ1020





The following conditions need to be met for the expansion solution using SSDs, which are the basic requirements for the expansion to be proven to be successful.

reComputer for Jetson:

JetPack versions 4.4 ~ 4.6
Carrier board must contain M.2 M-Key slot

SSD:

SSD need to be fourth generation extended file system (Ext4)
M.2 M-Key interface with NVMe protocol
Recommended capacity ≤ 512 GB







Follow the steps in the Hardware Instructions to install the SSD for reComputer.



Use the shortcut Ctrl+F or click the Ubuntu icon in the upper left corner to search for Disks and open the Disks tool that comes with Ubuntu 18.04.





Select your SSD on the left side and then select Format Disk in the upper right corner under the menu bar.





Format your SSD to GPT format. A pop-up window will appear asking you to confirm and enter your user password.





Then, we click on the middle “+” to add a disk character.





Click on “Next”





Please give your SSD a name and select Ext4 in the type and click “Create”. At this point we have completed the SSD prep according to the expansion requirements.








Use the git command to download the script files we need to use to reComputer.
git clone https://github.com/limengdu/rootOnNVMe.git
cd rootOnNVMe/
Then execute the following command to build the files from the root directory in the eMMC to the SSD, the wait time for this step depends on the size of the root directory you are using.
./copy-rootfs-ssd.sh



Execute the following command to complete the configuration of rootfs.
./setup-service.sh





When you restart reComputer, you will see that the eMMC has become an external storage device on the main interface, and you will see that the system footprint has been reduced, so the expansion was successful.





!!!Attention The default SSD path in the script file is /dev/nvme0n1p1, which is also the path assigned by default by reComputer. If you find that your SSD path does not match this with the command sudo fdisk -l, change the path of all /dev/nvme0n1p1 in the files copy-rootfs-ssd.sh, data/setssdroot.service, and data/setssdroot.sh in rootOnNVMe to the path where your SSD is located.





The above expansion will not remove the original root directory contents from the eMMC. If you do not want to boot from the SSD, you can remove the SSD and the system will still boot from the eMMC.

title: Flashing JetPack OS via Command Line
text:
Flashing JetPack OS via command line can be very easy for the Linux knowledge base users.


On the Linux host PC, we need to open a browser and go the Jetson Linux Archive. First we should check if the version of Jetson Linux is supported our reComputer Jetson module.





For ReCompute the latest version used was 32.7.4. Once you find the proper version, click to go to the downloaded page. Find and click the “L4T Driver Package (BSP)” and “Sample Root Filesystem” to download the driver files. The names of the files are like Tegra_Linux_Sample-Root-Filesystem_Rxx.x.x_aarch64.tbz2 and Jetson-210_Linux_Rxx.x.x_aarch64.tbz2.





As the example, we choose the NVIDIA L4T 35.1 version since it is included as part of JetPack 5.0.2 and supports the Jetson Xavier NX module. The names of the files:

Tegra_Linux_Sample-Root-Filesystem_R35.1.0_aarch64.tbz2
Jetson_Linux_R35.1.0_aarch64.tbz2







NoteINFO



You can also choose other version like NVIDIA L4T 32.7.2 which supports Jetpack 4.6.2.





mkdir -p ~/jetson_nano_flash
cd ~/jetson_nano_flash
# Place both downloaded files here
On the Linux host PC, we should find a folder and store the package files we download before. Then open a command line window(Terminal) at the folder and use the command line below to unzip the files and assemble the rootfs:
tar xf ${L4T_RELEASE_PACKAGE}
cd Linux_for_Tegra/rootfs/
sudo tar xpf ../../${SAMPLE_FS_PACKAGE}
cd ..
sudo ./apply_binaries.sh






NoteNOTE



${} is where you put the names of the files.


As the example of NVIDIA L4T 35.1, the downloaded files are stored in /Desktop/L4T_Drivers, so under the ‘/Desktop/L4T_Drivers’ path we open the command line window(Terminal) and execute the following command.
tar xf Jetson_Linux_R35.1.0_aarch64.tbz2
cd Linux_for_Tegra/rootfs/
sudo tar xpf ../../Tegra_Linux_Sample-Root-Filesystem_R35.1.0_aarch64.tbz2
cd ..
sudo ./apply_binaries.sh
The output should be like:








Since we alreadly force the reComputer J2021 into the recovery mode and the module is Jetson Xavier NX. We can directly flash the system into the reComputer execute following command:
sudo ./flash.sh jetson-nano-emmc mmcblk0p1











NoteNOTE



Flashing L4T takes about 10 minutes, or more under a slow host computer.


At this moment, we can unplug the jumper and then power up the reComputer again to use it.




It is mandatory that the Host be a Linux Machine version 18.04, since if the machine does not have this operating system the flashing will not work.
QEMU binary is not available, looking for QEMU from host system: To solve this, follow the next commands

sudo apt update
sudo apt install qemu-user-static




Do not use virtual machines to do this process, either by command line or via SDK Manager
If you do not have a machine with Linux Ubuntu 18.04 you will need to get one, or failing that install the operating system on your machine, you can do this by dual boot following the next resource:

Windows and Linux in one PC

For more information refer to documentation

Seeed Studio Wiki

title: HAR Distributed Framework
text:
Welcome to the technical documentation of the HAR Distributed Framework, a distributed wearable computing system developed for Real-Time Human Activity Recognition (HAR) using embedded computing devices and wearable inertial sensors.
This website documents the design, implementation, configuration, deployment, and experimental evaluation of the complete framework.
The main purpose of this documentation is to provide the technical information required to understand how the system was built and to facilitate its reproduction, extension, and adaptation for future research.


The documentation covers the complete development workflow of the system, including:

Wearable Sensing and Data Acquisition
Embedded Computing Infrastructure
Dataset Preparation and Preprocessing
Local Neural Network Development
Distributed Inference
Probability-Level Communication
Multi-Node Synchronization
Central Prediction Fusion
Real-Time Deployment
System Monitoring and Logging
Graphical Visualization
Experimental Evaluation
Centralized And Distributed Configurations
Robustness Experiments
Result Reproduction




The system follows a distributed inference architecture in which wearable sensor data are processed close to their source using embedded edge devices. Each edge device executes a local Human Activity Recognition model and transmits class probability vectors rather than continuous raw sensor streams. These predictions are collected by a central node, synchronized, and combined to produce the final global activity prediction.

title: Software Environment
text:
The HAR Distributed Framework relies on a software stack that supports wearable sensor acquisition, embedded neural network inference, distributed communication, synchronization, experiment logging, and real-time visualization.
Because the framework operates across multiple embedded computing devices, the software environment must also provide a consistent mechanism for deploying and executing the required components on independent nodes.
The principal software technologies used by the framework include:

title: Software Environment
text:
Software Architecture
The software stack can be viewed as a set of layers running on top of the distributed hardware infrastructure:
Application Layer
────────────────────────────────────────
HAR Models
Sensor Acquisition
Central Fusion
Logging
Visualization

Distributed Middleware
────────────────────────────────────────
ROS Noetic

Runtime Environment
────────────────────────────────────────
Python
PyTorch
CUDA

Containerization
────────────────────────────────────────
Docker

Operating System
────────────────────────────────────────
Linux / NVIDIA Jetson Environment

Hardware
────────────────────────────────────────
Jetson Edge Nodes + Central Jetson
Not every component is executed on every device.
The edge nodes primarily execute sensor acquisition and local inference, while the central node executes synchronization, prediction fusion, experiment logging, and communication with higher-level visualization components.

title: Software Environment
text:
Distributed Software Roles
The software responsibilities are distributed according to the role of each computing node.

Edge Nodes
Each edge node is responsible for running the software required to:

communicate with its associated wearable sensor;
acquire incoming sensor measurements;
buffer sensor data;
construct input windows;
execute a local HAR neural network;
generate activity probability vectors;
publish predictions through ROS;
timestamp prediction messages; and
record local performance information when required.

Conceptually:
Linux
  │
Docker
  │
ROS + Python + PyTorch
  │
  ├── Sensor Acquisition
  ├── Data Buffering
  ├── Local Inference
  └── Prediction Publisher


Central Node
The central computing node executes the software responsible for:

receiving predictions from all distributed nodes;
synchronizing incoming prediction messages;
handling temporarily unavailable predictions;
executing the central fusion model;
publishing global predictions;
recording timing and synchronization metrics; and
communicating with the visualization interface.

Conceptually:
Linux
  │
Docker
  │
ROS + Python + PyTorch
  │
  ├── Prediction Subscribers
  ├── Synchronization
  ├── Fusion Model
  ├── Global Prediction
  └── Experiment Logging

title: Software Environment
text:
Containerized Deployment
Docker is used to provide isolated and reproducible execution environments across the distributed embedded devices.
Rather than configuring every framework dependency directly in the host operating system, the main runtime components can be executed inside containers.
The general deployment structure is:
Jetson Host System
       │
       ▼
     Docker
       │
       ▼
HAR Container
       │
       ├── ROS Noetic
       ├── Python
       ├── HAR Software
       ├── Model Files
       └── Required Dependencies
Containerization provides a consistent software environment across different computing nodes and simplifies deployment of the distributed ROS-based system.
The exact Docker configuration, container creation procedure, device access, networking options, and execution commands are documented separately.

title: Software Environment
text:
ROS Noetic
The distributed communication layer is implemented using ROS Noetic.
ROS provides the publish/subscribe infrastructure used to exchange prediction information between the five local edge nodes and the central computing node.
The communication architecture follows the general structure:
Local Edge Nodes
      │
      │ ROS Topics
      ▼
Central Node
      │
      ▼
Global Prediction
Each local node publishes its probability predictions through a dedicated ROS topic.
The central node subscribes to the distributed prediction streams and processes them as part of the synchronization and fusion pipeline.
ROS is also used to distribute control and visualization-related information within the framework.
Detailed documentation of the ROS architecture is provided later under the Communication Framework section.

title: Software Environment
Software Environment
text:
PyTorch
The neural network models used by the framework are implemented and executed using PyTorch.
PyTorch is used for:

loading trained model parameters;
preparing model inputs;
executing local neural network inference;
executing the central fusion model; and
GPU-accelerated inference where supported by the target platform.

A previously evaluated centralized GPU environment used:
PyTorch 2.0.0+nv23.05
CUDA 11.4
These versions correspond to that specific centralized deployment and should not automatically be assumed to represent every Jetson node in the distributed system.
The exact software configuration for each platform will therefore be documented independently where necessary.

title: Software Environment
text:
GPU Acceleration
NVIDIA Jetson platforms provide integrated GPU resources that can be used by supported machine learning frameworks.
Where GPU acceleration is enabled, the software stack conceptually becomes:
HAR Application
      │
      ▼
   PyTorch
      │
      ▼
    CUDA
      │
      ▼
NVIDIA GPU
The use of GPU acceleration depends on the model, platform, runtime environment, and installed NVIDIA software stack.
The deployment section will document how model execution was configured on the corresponding embedded platforms.

title: Software Environment
text:
Clock Synchronization Software
The framework requires synchronized system clocks because predictions are generated independently across multiple physical devices.
Chrony is used to maintain clock synchronization between the central node and the distributed edge nodes.
Conceptually:
                 Central Node
                 Time Reference
                      │
        ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
        │             │             │
        ▼             ▼             ▼
     Edge 1        Edge 2        Edge 3
        │             │             │
        ▼             ▼             ▼
     Edge 4        Edge 5       synchronized
                                  timestamps
Synchronized timestamps are subsequently used by the communication and experiment measurement mechanisms.
The complete Chrony configuration will be documented as a dedicated procedure.

title: Software Environment
text:
Visualization Software
A graphical visualization interface was developed using Unity.
The interface receives global HAR information from the distributed system and provides a real-time representation of system predictions.
The high-level communication path is:
Distributed Edge Nodes
         │
         ▼
     Central Node
         │
         ▼
  Global Prediction
         │
         ▼
       Unity
         │
         ▼
Real-Time Visualization
The Unity interface is not required for the core HAR inference process but provides a useful mechanism for observing system behavior during real-time experiments.
Its installation, ROS connectivity, activity visualization, and animation configuration are documented separately.
